'''Geranium molle''', the '''dove's-foot crane's-bill'''<ref>{{Citation |year=2007 |title=BSBI 2007 list |publisher=Botanical Society of the British Isles |url=http://www.bsbi.org.uk/BSBI2007.xls |accessdate=2012-02-02 |url-status=dead |archiveurl=http://arquivo.pt/wayback/20090707234654/http%3A//www.bsbi.org.uk/BSBI2007.xls |archivedate=2009-07-07 }}</ref> or '''dovesfoot geranium''',<ref>{{Citation |year=1994 |title=Plants of Coastal British Columbia |author=Pojar and MacKinnon}}</ref> is an [[Annual plant|annual]] [[herbaceous]] plant of the family [[Geraniaceae]].

== Description ==
''Geranium molle'' is a small plant reaching on average {{convert|5|-|30|cm}} in height.<ref name=Pignatti>Pignatti S. - Flora d'Italia – Edagricole – 1982. Vol. II, pag. 10</ref> It is a very branched plant, quite [[Trichome|hairy]], with several ascending stems. The leaves are palmate, cut 5 to 9 times. The basal leaves are arranged in a rosette, the upper ones are sessile, rounded and hairy, with a long petiole of about {{convert|5|-|12|mm}}.<ref name=Pignatti/> The flowers are pinkish-purple, 8–12 mm in diameter, with very jagged petals. It blooms from April to September. The flowers are [[Glossary of botanical terms|hermaphrodite]] and mainly pollinated by [[Hymenoptera]]. Fruits are glabrous, usually with 6-9 transverse ridges.<ref name=Pignatti/>

==Distribution and habitat==
It is native to the Mediterranean and sub-Mediterranean areas, but has naturalized in other parts of [[Europe]], in southwestern and central  Asia and in North Africa, though it may have already been in those parts and areas, just not properly identified.{{citation needed|date=February 2018}} It is considered an [[introduced species]] in North America, where it is known as '''Dovefoot Geranium''' or '''Awnless Geranium'''. Although non-native in parts of its range, this species poses little threat to native ecosystems.<ref>E-FLORA BC: ELECTRONIC ATLAS OF THE FLORA OF BRITISH COLUMBIA</ref>

It is found in dry meadows, hedges, banks and forest edges. It prefers sunny places on sandy and relatively dry soils,  at an altitude of {{convert|0|-|1000|m}} above sea level.<ref name=Pignatti/>

==Herbal medicine==
[[Nicholas Culpeper]] in his herbal of 1652 suggested a variety of uses for ''G. molle'', including the treatment of internal and external injuries. A note was made that the bruised leaf healed external injuries faster. A decoction in wine was said to relieve gout and other joint pains.<ref>{{Citation |last1=Culpeper |first1=Nicholas |title=The English physitian: or an astrologo-physical discourse of the vulgar herbs of this nation |location=London |publisher=Peter Cole |year=1652}}</ref>
